findings.mechanism: Per‑request httpx.AsyncClient prevents connection reuse, so each call incurs a full TLS handshake and loses the benefits of a connection pool (reference: "A connection pool is a queue with a hard capacity … usually two or three pools are stacked … the narrowest one sets the real concurrency").
findings.remediation: Instantiate a single httpx.AsyncClient at module load time (or reuse a client pool) and reuse it for all charge calls.
findings.arithmetic: Typical TLS handshake ≈100 ms per new TCP/TLS connection. Because a new client (and thus a new connection) is created on every request, the 99th‑percentile request latency is increased by at least 100 ms regardless of load.

findings.mechanism: The client timeout of 10 s can block a worker for the full duration of a slow upstream response; with 4 uvicorn workers the maximum sustainable arrival rate is workers/timeout = 4/10 s = 0.4 rps. Higher arrival rates will cause requests to queue (reference: "When demand exceeds capacity requests do not fail, they wait … the narrowest one sets the real concurrency").
findings.remediation: Set a client timeout that is shorter than the service’s overall deadline and align it with the expected upstream latency; optionally configure a connection‑pool limit that matches the worker count.
findings.arithmetic: Throughput = workers / timeout = 4 / 10 s = 0.4 rps. Any arrival rate >0.4 rps leads to worker saturation (worker_saturation → 1) and queue depth growth.
